slides.title: Chapter Contract
slides.notes: Open by treating the first page as a contract for the entire course. The students should hear that this lecture is not a catalog of layer names. It is a method for asking what object carries the data, which transformations preserve meaning, and what a model is required to respect.

slides.title: Representation Learning
slides.notes: Emphasize that representation learning is useful because the raw coordinates are rarely the final explanatory space. A model learns a feature map, but the geometric question is what the map is allowed to forget, what it must preserve, and how the downstream readout uses that organized information.

slides.title: Structured Data
slides.notes: Make the contrast with ambient vectors concrete. The same number of coordinates can describe pixels, graph nodes, sampled points, or time steps, but those coordinates come with different adjacency, motion, and relabeling rules. The domain is therefore part of the data, not decoration around the data.

slides.title: Symmetry Preview
slides.notes: Use the commuting square as the first durable mental model. If an input is transformed, an equivariant map transforms the output in the matching way, while an invariant map makes the output unchanged. The lecture only previews the formalism, but students should already see the residual as a testable claim.

slides.title: Locality And Sharing
slides.notes: Connect locality to parameter discipline rather than to a single architecture. A local rule sees a neighborhood, and sharing applies the same rule across comparable neighborhoods. This explains why convolutions, message passing, and attention variants can all be read as ways to control how information moves.

slides.title: The GDL Design Loop
slides.notes: Walk through the loop clockwise and ask for a decision at each stop. Identify the domain, name the transformations, choose invariant or equivariant behavior, build a local shared operator, and then check the residual. The point is that geometric deep learning is a design loop with audits.

slides.title: Three Example Readouts
slides.notes: Read the three examples as different answers to the same design questions. A classifier wants invariance to image translation, a node predictor wants equivariance to graph relabeling, and a point cloud energy wants rigid motion invariance. The model family changes because the target behavior changes.

slides.title: Failure Mode
slides.notes: Use this warning as a practical diagnostic. If relabeling a graph changes a graph-level answer, the network has learned from names instead of structure. If rotation changes a molecular energy, the representation is leaking coordinates. The residual gauge turns a vague modeling worry into a visible failure.

slides.title: Notebook Audit Trail
slides.notes: Point students to the notebook as the executable companion to the lecture. The generated visuals use synthetic data so every claim can be inspected, and the JSON ledgers record small residual checks. This makes the chapter a reproducible laboratory rather than a passive introduction.

slides.title: Takeaway
slides.notes: Close by returning to the four chapter ideas in one sentence. Representation learning builds useful internal coordinates, structured data supplies the domain, symmetry predicts which changes matter, and the GDL loop turns these choices into architecture and checks. The rest of the course repeats this pattern at higher resolution.
